## Overview

The Nansemond are the Indigenous nation of the Nansemond River, a 20-mile-long tributary of the James River in Virginia. They traditionally lived in settlements on both sides of the river, where they fished, harvested oysters, hunted, and farmed fertile soil. The name “Nansemond” means “fishing point” in Algonquian. Today, Nansemond people belong to the federally recognized Nansemond Indian Nation, and many members live on ancestral lands in Suffolk, Chesapeake, and surrounding cities. The Nation has about 400 tribal members. Nansemond history includes membership in the Powhatan Confederacy, displacement during European colonization, cultural continuity through periods of discrimination, and efforts to restore ancestral places such as Mattanock.

## Material culture

### Architecture

Nansemond houses were known as *yehakins*. The sources describe houses being ransacked during the conflict of 1609. The Nansemond weroance lived on Dumpling Island, where a “temple” housed sacred items and burial sites of weroances were located. The Nation later planned to reconstruct Mattanock Town using archaeological and other research so that longhouses and other structures would match historical dimensions. The planned site also included a community center, museum, and pow wow ground. In 2013, the City of Suffolk transferred about 70 acres of riverfront property along the Nansemond River to the Nansemond, but the city repossessed the property after the planned tourist village was not completed within the required period. On May 15, 2024, the Suffolk City Council approved a Memorandum of Understanding allowing 71 acres to be transferred back to the Nation, with conservation and education prioritized over tourism.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources mention pearls and copper items as valuables customarily buried with the bodies of weroances. In 1609, Jamestown settlers attempted to trade ratchets and copper for food. Mussel shells were described in connection with the cutting and scraping of the brains of missing colonists.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources mention pearls and copper items, which were customarily buried with the bodies of weroances.

## Music & performance

The sources do record that the Nansemond Nation hosts a powwow every year in August and that the planned restoration of Mattanock Town included a pow wow ground.

## Festivals & rituals

The Nansemond Nation hosts a powwow every year in August. In November 2013, members of the Nansemond Tribe gathered at the historic site of Mattanock Town and blessed the land after the City of Suffolk transferred ancestral lands back to the tribe.

The sources describe sacred places and funerary practices in the early seventeenth century. Dumpling Island was the location of the weroance’s residence and of a “temple” housing sacred items. Burial sites of weroances and their sacred items were destroyed during a colonial raid. Pearls and copper items were customarily buried with weroances’ bodies.

John Bass married Elizabeth, the daughter of the leader of the Nansemond Nation, on August 14, 1638, after she was baptized into the established Anglican Church of the colony.

## Foodways

Nansemond people traditionally fished, harvested oysters, hunted, and farmed in fertile soil. In 1609, Jamestown settlers attempted to trade ratchets and copper for food.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Nansemond language article states that several Nansemond words were historically documented by John Smith and that only six words have been preserved. These include nĭkătwĭn, näkătwĭn, nikwásăti, toisíaw’, mishä́naw, and marímo. The sources state that the words may have been corrupted in memory by the time they were written down in 1901. They also record the terms *Mattanock*, *Chuckatuck*, *Weyhohomo*, and *Pochick*.

The restoration of Mattanock Town was planned to use archaeological and other research, with the aim of demonstrating Nansemond heritage.

## Language & religion

The Nansemond language is extinct and was spoken by the Nansemond people of Virginia. It may have belonged to the Algonquian language family, similar to the languages of other Atlantic coastal tribes, but only six words have been preserved, which are not enough to identify and classify it. The recorded words are nĭkătwĭn “one,” näkătwĭn “two,” nikwásăti “three,” toisíaw’ “four,” mishä́naw “five,” and marímo “dog.” The Nansemond language article also records *Pochick* as meaning non-Christian/Nansemond.

The Nansemond weroancy belonged to the Powhatan Confederacy, which was led by the Mamanatowick, also known as the Powhatan, and by the weroances of its various weroancies. Some Nansemond became Christians and adopted European manners of living. Elizabeth, daughter of the Nansemond leader, was baptized into the established Anglican Church before her marriage in 1638. The sources also state that tribal members who were Catholic continued to be registered by churches as Indian for baptisms, marriages, and funerals. The Indiana United Methodist Church was founded in 1850 as a mission for the Nansemond.

- The sources supplied for this profile contain no museum catalogue records for Nansemond objects.

commons_photos.description: The in the foreground, with the sunglasses, confronted me later in the day asking me why I was only taking photos of dark skin Indians.  I told her I am sure I got a photo of her, that I take photos of everyone.  She said I was not telling the truth, she had seen me lower the camera every time the "white Natives" walked by, and she is a Nansemond Indian by blood.  I told her she was mistaken, but I took photos of her and the woman next to her and sent them to her along with this photo.
